claims.text: The starting CoCrFeNi alloy has a typical coarse-grained microstructure.
The starting CoCrFeNi alloy has no pre-existing self-lubricating surface layer.
Controlled high-energy mechanical surface treatment can produce an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer in CoCrFeNi.
Controlled high-energy mechanical surface treatment can produce a partially amorphous near-surface layer in CoCrFeNi.
The ultra-nanocrystalline or amorphized layer has reduced shear strength associated with inverse Hall-Petch behavior.
Specific high-angle grain-boundary characteristics contribute to the behavior of the engineered layer.
The engineered layer promotes dissipative deformation under sliding.
Cavitation-induced nanoporosity may develop in the highly deformed near-surface layer.
Dissipative deformation and nanoporosity reduce the effective shear resistance of the surface.
The structural transformation produces self-lubricating behavior.
The treated CoCrFeNi alloy will maintain lower friction than untreated CoCrFeNi from room temperature to 800 °C.
The treated alloy's coefficient of friction will approach or fall below approximately 0.3 throughout the stated temperature range.
The treated CoCrFeNi alloy will maintain lower wear rates than untreated CoCrFeNi from room temperature to 800 °C.
The treatment will improve wear volume by approximately one order of magnitude relative to untreated CoCrFeNi.
Untreated CoCrFeNi typically experiences increased friction at higher temperatures because it lacks an engineered lubricious surface layer.
Untreated CoCrFeNi typically experiences increased wear at higher temperatures because it lacks an engineered lubricious surface layer.
The intervention is effective from 25 °C to 800 °C under sliding loads comparable to prior studies in an inert or controlled atmosphere.
Performance under oxidative environments or drastically different loads is uncertain.
The long-term stability of the induced layer under repeated sliding cycles is unresolved.
A greater than 20% statistically significant reduction in both friction coefficient and wear rate across the full range is the minimum performance criterion used to avoid falsification.

contradictions.description: The predicted wear outcome is an order-of-magnitude improvement, whereas the falsification rule accepts any statistically significant improvement greater than 20%; thus an outcome far below the stated prediction could still avoid falsification.
